questions.prompt: `async function count() { return 1; }` What is `const x = count();`?

choices.text: The number `1`
`undefined`, because the function hasn't finished
A `Promise<number>` that resolves to `1`
A compile error, because `count` has no `await`

questions.explanation: An `async` function always returns a promise. A returned value that isn't a promise is wrapped, as if by `Promise.resolve(1)`. To get the number, `await count()` or use `.then`. `async` functions don't need to contain `await`.

sources.title: async function - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: An async function always returns a promise, a non-promise return value is wrapped as if by Promise.resolve, and it may contain zero await expressions.

questions.prompt: `slow()` resolves after 2 s and `fast()` after 1 s; they don't depend on each other. How long does `const a = await slow(); const b = await fast();` take, and how do you make it about 2 s?

choices.text: About 2 s already, because both run in the background
About 3 s; start both, then `await Promise.all([slow(), fast()])`
About 3 s; add `async` to the caller to run them together
About 1 s, because `fast` finishes first

questions.explanation: `await` pauses until the promise settles, so `fast()` doesn't start until `slow()` has finished: 2 + 1 = 3 s. Calling both before awaiting runs them at the same time. `Promise.all` is the safe way to await both, because it also handles the case where one rejects early.

sources.title: async function - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: Awaiting a 2 s and a 1 s promise one after the other takes about 3 s, while starting both and awaiting Promise.all takes about 2 s and handles rejections safely.

sources.title: Promise.all() - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects, with that first reason.

questions.prompt: `await Promise.all([search(), fetchDocs(), lookupUser()])`: `fetchDocs()` rejects after 100 ms, and the other two succeed later. What happens?

choices.text: `Promise.all` waits for all three and then rejects with an array of the errors
It resolves once all settle, with `undefined` in `fetchDocs`'s position
It rejects about 100 ms in and cancels `search()` and `lookupUser()`
It rejects about 100 ms in with `fetchDocs`'s error; the others keep running

questions.explanation: `Promise.all` fails fast: it rejects as soon as any input rejects, with that first reason. It can't cancel the other operations; they run to completion and their results are ignored. To cancel them you need something like an `AbortController`; to get every outcome, use `Promise.allSettled`.

sources.title: Promise.all() - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: Promise.all rejects immediately when any input rejects, with the first rejection reason, and rejecting does not cancel the remaining operations.

questions.prompt: `Promise.all([a(), b(), c()])` where `c()` finishes first and `a()` last. In what order are the results?

choices.text: `[a, b, c]`: input order, whatever order they finished in
`[c, b, a]`: the order they finished in, fastest first
An order that varies from run to run, depending on timing
Sorted by how long each took, shortest first

questions.explanation: MDN: the fulfilled value is an array in the order of the promises passed, regardless of completion order. So you can destructure the results, `const [x, y, z] = await Promise.all(...)`, safely.

sources.title: Promise.all() - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: The fulfilment value is an array in the order of the promises passed, regardless of completion order.

questions.prompt: Your agent runs three independent tool calls at the same time. Would you use `Promise.all` or `Promise.allSettled`? Explain the trade-off.

model_answer.summary: `Promise.all` is right when one failure makes the whole step useless; `Promise.allSettled` is right when partial results are still worth returning to the model, which is common for independent tools.
key_points: Both run the calls concurrently and keep results in input order
`Promise.all` rejects at the first rejection, so you lose the other results
`Promise.allSettled` waits for all of them and gives `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }` for each, so the model can get the successes and the errors
Neither cancels calls that are still running; use an `AbortController` (and timeouts) for that

questions.explanation: For an agent, a failed tool is usually information for the model ("search failed, try again") rather than a reason to abort the whole step, which makes `allSettled` the common choice.

sources.title: Promise.all() - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: Promise.all fails fast on the first rejection without cancelling other operations, whereas allSettled waits for every input.

sources.title: Promise.allSettled() - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: allSettled fulfils with one {status, value} or {status, reason} object per input, in input order.

questions.prompt: Under `"strict": true` (TypeScript 4.4+), what does the compiler say about `try { await callModel(); } catch (err) { console.log(err.message); }`?

choices.text: Nothing: `err` is typed `Error`, so `.message` is safe
Nothing: `catch` variables are `any`, even under `strict`
An error: `await` isn't allowed inside a `try` block that has a `catch` clause
An error: `err` is `unknown`; narrow it, for example with `instanceof Error`

questions.explanation: `strict` turns on `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, so `catch` variables are `unknown` instead of `any`. JavaScript can throw any value, not only `Error` objects, so you narrow with `instanceof Error` before reading `.message`.

sources.title: TypeScript: TSConfig Reference
sources.claim: strict enables useUnknownInCatchVariables (added in TypeScript 4.4), which types catch variables as unknown instead of any so you must check it is an Error before using it.

questions.prompt: `async function load() { try { return fetchJson(url); } catch { return null; } }` `fetchJson` returns a promise that rejects. What does `await load()` do?

choices.text: It returns `null`, because the `catch` handles the returned promise's later rejection
It rejects: the promise isn't awaited, so it rejects after the `try` has finished
It returns `undefined`, because `try` swallows the returned promise
It fails to compile: `return` of a promise isn't allowed inside `try`

questions.explanation: `try`/`catch` only catches what goes wrong while the `try` block runs. `return fetchJson(url)` hands the pending promise back immediately, so the `try` block completes, and the promise rejects later. Write `return await fetchJson(url)` so the rejection is thrown inside the `try` and caught.

sources.title: await - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: return await unwraps the promise so its rejection is thrown inside the current function, unlike returning the promise directly, and return await is almost always preferable.

sources.title: async function - JavaScript | MDN
sources.claim: A returned promise becomes the async function's result and is not awaited, so the try/catch only covers errors raised at await points inside the try block.

questions.prompt: You validate a model's reply with `const r = Answer.safeParse(data)`. The data doesn't match the schema. What do you get?

choices.text: It throws a `ZodError` whose `issues` list each problem
`{ success: false, error }`; `error.issues` lists each problem with its path
`{ success: true, data }`, with the invalid fields silently stripped from `data`
`r` is `undefined`, and you call `Answer.parse` to see why

questions.explanation: `safeParse` never throws for invalid data: it returns a discriminated union, `{ success: true, data }` or `{ success: false, error }`. `.parse` returns the validated data or throws a `ZodError`. In an agent loop `safeParse` fits better, because a bad reply is expected and you want to act on the issues.

sources.title: Basic usage | Zod
sources.claim: safeParse returns a discriminated union result object with success and either data or a ZodError whose issues list each problem with its path.

questions.prompt: Walk through how you validate an LLM's JSON output with Zod in TypeScript, from the raw text to a typed value, including what you do when validation fails.

model_answer.summary: Parse the text with `JSON.parse` inside a `try`, check the result with the schema's `safeParse`, and use the typed `data` on success. On failure, send the issues back to the model for a bounded retry, or fail clearly.
key_points: `JSON.parse` the text inside `try`/`catch`, because invalid JSON throws
Treat the parsed value as `unknown` and run `Schema.safeParse(value)`
On success, use `result.data`, whose type comes from `z.infer<typeof Schema>`
On failure, send `result.error.issues` back to the model and retry a limited number of times, or return an error
Run-time validation is needed because TypeScript types are erased and can't check data at run time

questions.explanation: A TypeScript type only describes what you hope arrives. The Zod schema is what checks it, and `z.infer` keeps the type and the check from drifting apart.

sources.title: Basic usage | Zod
sources.claim: safeParse returns success/data or error with issues, and z.infer extracts the static type from a schema.

questions.prompt: Compare Zod's `.parse` and `.safeParse`. Which would you use to validate model output inside an agent loop, and which for your app's own config file?

model_answer.summary: `.parse` throws on invalid data, which suits data that should never be wrong. `.safeParse` returns a result object, which suits data that is often wrong, such as model output.
key_points: `.parse` returns a validated, typed deep clone of the input, or throws a `ZodError`
`.safeParse` doesn't throw on invalid data: it returns `{ success: true, data }` or `{ success: false, error }`
Model output is often invalid, so `.safeParse` makes failure an ordinary branch where you can retry with the issues
A bad config file is a bug to stop on at startup, so `.parse` and its exception fit
Schemas with async refinements or transforms need `parseAsync` or `safeParseAsync`

questions.explanation: Choose based on whether invalid data is expected. Exceptions are for surprises; model output failing validation is not a surprise.

sources.title: Basic usage | Zod
sources.claim: .parse returns a strongly typed deep clone or throws a ZodError, .safeParse returns a result object instead of throwing, and async refinements or transforms need parseAsync or safeParseAsync.

questions.prompt: `const Answer = z.object({ answer: z.string(), confidence: z.number().optional() }); type Answer = z.infer<typeof Answer>;` What is `Answer`?

choices.text: `{ answer: string; confidence: number }`
`{ answer: string; confidence: number | null }`
`{ answer: string; confidence?: number | undefined }`
`{ answer: unknown; confidence: unknown }`

questions.explanation: `.optional()` allows `undefined`, and `z.infer` turns it into an optional property. You write the shape once, as a schema, and get both the run-time check and the static type from it. Allowing `null` would need `.nullable()`.

sources.title: Defining schemas | Zod
sources.claim: An .optional() object field infers as an optional property typed value | undefined, and .nullable() is what allows null.

sources.title: Basic usage | Zod
sources.claim: z.infer extracts the static TypeScript type from a schema.

questions.prompt: `z.object({ answer: z.string() }).parse({ answer: "42", note: "extra" })` returns what?

choices.text: `{ answer: "42" }`, because unknown keys are stripped by default
`{ answer: "42", note: "extra" }`, because unknown keys pass through
It throws, because `note` isn't in the schema
It throws, because `"42"` isn't a number

questions.explanation: By default `z.object` strips unrecognised keys from the result. `z.strictObject` throws on unknown keys, and `z.looseObject` lets them through. For model output, stripping keeps extra fields the model invented out of your code; use `strictObject` when an extra key should count as a failure.

sources.title: Defining schemas | Zod
sources.claim: z.object strips unrecognised keys by default; z.strictObject throws on unknown keys and z.looseObject passes them through.
